title: Require a documented legal basis and meaningful human review before an automated system informs an adverse decision about a person's rights or benefits
description: Illustrative reference decision modelled on three documented government automated-decision failures: the Dutch SyRI/childcare-benefits scandal, the UK Ofqual grading algorithm, and Australia's Robodebt scheme. Not a documented decision of any specific organization.

history.note: Initial Phase 2A seed content, part of the Foundational Twenty.

Normalized US/UK spelling variants to the American-English house style (schema field names, e.g. organizations_involved, are already American; majority framework citations - NIST, FTC, EEOC, FCRA, BIPA - are American sources). Normalized a duplicated relationship-reason phrasing ("...via this design pattern." -> "...via this single, primary design pattern.") to one canonical wording.

decision_statement: Before an automated or algorithmic system is used to make or materially inform a decision that adversely affects a person's welfare eligibility, exam results, immigration status, or similar legal rights, the organization must document the legal basis for the processing, complete a data protection impact assessment, and guarantee the affected person a right to meaningful human review before the decision takes effect — not merely an appeals process after harm has occurred.
decision_context: Motivated by three independent, well-documented government automated-decision failures across three countries, each involving an algorithm making or heavily informing an adverse decision about individuals' welfare, education, or benefits without adequate legal basis, impact assessment, or a genuine human-review safeguard before harm occurred.
governing_body: Illustrative example — Public Sector Automated Decision-Making Governance Board
alternatives_considered: Rely on a post-hoc appeals process rather than pre-decision human review.
Treat impact assessment as a one-time exercise rather than repeating it when the system or its data changes.

relationships.reason: This decision is modelled as a direct governance response to this incident, the most severe of the three.
The decision is put into practice via this single, primary design pattern.
A guaranteed pre-decision human-review right is the core mechanism satisfying this control.
Compliance must be demonstrated by a completed data protection impact assessment.
Boards adopting this decision should be asking whether affected individuals can actually obtain human review, not just theoretically request it.
